structure.title: Debts to others
structure.text: Book 1 recalls people from whom Marcus learned habits and values. It gives the later self-admonitions a social background.

structure.title: Repeated practice
structure.text: Books 2–12 return to judgment, duty, mortality, and other people without forming a continuous treatise. Read the repetitions as renewed exercises.

people.name: Judgment
people.text: The interpretation attached to an event.

people.name: Duty
people.text: Action appropriate to one's place among others.

people.name: Nature
people.text: The larger order within which Marcus understands a human life.

context.title: Notes to himself
context.text: Marcus is repeatedly addressing his own failures of attention and conduct. A severe sentence may be a corrective aimed at a particular weakness.
context.takeaway: Hear the self-address before turning it into advice.

context.title: Stoic belonging
context.text: Stoicism joins discipline of judgment to obligations towards other people. Detachment from praise does not automatically mean withdrawal from public life.

notice.why: Repetition reveals how difficult the desired habits remain.

passages.quote: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody

notice.why: Images of cosmic time loosen the hold of immediate anxieties.

opening: Marcus Aurelius commanded an empire, but he still had to talk himself into getting out of bed. Stoic philosophy gave him arguments for doing his work, enduring discomfort, and dealing with people who annoyed him. In these private notes he returns to the same difficulties, sometimes patiently, sometimes with the severity of someone tired of his own excuses. An emperor’s authority could make other people obey; it could not spare him the daily effort of governing his own temper and desires.
